title: How households and school communities adapt behaviour after waste-disposal charging and stronger recycling expectations
reading_passage:
Role: Senior student editor.
Audience: Readers of the school sustainability bulletin (students, parents).
Purpose: Argue whether schools should mandate family practice logs for waste sorting to support municipal charging, or trust voluntary participation.

Stimulus: Estates report uneven compliance; some parents call logs intrusive. The EPD stresses education first.

Propose school-home communication that educates rather than polices.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 4)
interactive_tasks.answer:
Waste Logs: Good or Bad?

Many estates now have waste charging. Our school thinks about asking families to write logs about sorting. Some parents say this is too much work.

I think logs can help us learn habits, but they may make tired families angry. If we do logs, they should be simple and not every day.

Schools should encourage sorting by education, not by forcing parents. Maybe we can have workshops instead of strict logs.

In conclusion, I prefer voluntary participation first and see the results.
interactive_tasks.explanation: Clear position; basic linking; Limited range—Level 4.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 5)
interactive_tasks.answer:
Logs That Teach, Not Shame

Municipal charging has turned our rubbish bags into receipts of civic behaviour. Mandating family waste logs could deepen habits—or breed resentment if treated as surveillance homework.

Voluntary pilots with anonymised cohort data already show promise: students compare diversion trends without publishing which flat forgot labels. Compulsion should wait until estates distribute subsidised bag bundles and multilingual pictorial cards.

If logs arrive, anonymise, digitise lightly, and pair every tick-box with a one-page ‘why this bin’ rationale. Schools educate upstream; estates supply logistics. Anything else risks blaming cramped kitchens for policy designed for detached houses.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 5*)
interactive_tasks.answer:
Measurement Without Moral Panic

Accountability matters, but dignity matters too. Logs can scaffold reflection if framed as collective science—how our estate’s curve shifts—not as a parent report card.

The school’s role is translation: turn EPD guidelines into doable scripts for subdivided flats—rinse, drain, compress—rather than pristine Pinterest kitchens.

Recommend a staged mandate: first term voluntary dashboards; second term opt-in mentoring; only then consider light-touch household attestations for senior forms with consent protocols.

interactive_tasks.question: Model Answer (Level 5**)
interactive_tasks.answer:
The Ledger We Choose to Keep

Policy asks households to weigh wrappers; schools must weigh ethics. A log is not intrinsically coercive—paperwork becomes punitive only when we forget why we asked for it: to make waste legible, not families transparent.

I defend optional, anonymised logging tethered to tangible support: compost demos at kai-tak pop-ups, mobile bag dispensers, peer translators in Nepali and Bahasa. Pair every quantitative field with narrative space—‘what blocked you today?’—so stress surfaces as data, not discipline referrals.

If compulsion ever arrives, let it be collective: block-level goals co-signed by MCs and parent reps, not student homework. Otherwise schools risk exporting municipal failure into family shame—and calling it education.
interactive_tasks.explanation: Dense metaphor; systemic ethics; policy choreography—5**.
